intro: Thomas Knox’s concert-band arrangement gives the ballet’s enforced dance to brass, woodwind and percussion rather than the original full orchestra. Can you keep a steady pulse beneath the displaced accents?
question: Can you keep the pulse when the accents shift?

sections.label: Quiet restart
sections.mNote: earlier chromatic cells rebuild in a quieter, darker texture

cues.title: Kashchei’s enforced dance
cues.text: In the ballet, the Firebird compels Kashchei and his followers to dance. This recording uses Thomas Knox’s band arrangement; listen to the separated rhythmic gestures without assuming that an orchestral string section is present.
cues.evidence: The ballet scenario supplies the action, and Commons credits Knox’s arrangement for the United States Marine Band.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: From law to orchestration
cues.text: Stravinsky studied law in Saint Petersburg before pursuing his musical training privately with Rimsky-Korsakov. Their regular work on orchestration in 1905–08 preceded the commission for The Firebird.
cues.evidence: The Fondation Igor Stravinsky biography documents the law studies, private training and orchestration lessons.

cues.title: Accents across the pulse
cues.text: Follow the underlying pulse separately from the accented notes. The dance’s short figures can disturb your sense of where a strong beat belongs without making the pulse itself disappear.
cues.evidence: Displaced accents belong to the dance’s rhythmic writing; the analysis measures activity, not which notes a listener will hear as beats.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Paris, June 1910
cues.text: The Firebird opened at the Paris Opéra on 25 June 1910 for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes. Michel Fokine choreographed it and Tamara Karsavina danced the title role; Stravinsky had just turned twenty-eight.
cues.evidence: The Stravinsky Foundation dates the premiere and his birth; the documented premiere cast names Karsavina.

cues.title: A longer line within the dance
cues.text: The central span contrasts sustained writing with the earlier clipped gestures. Listen across the pulse for a longer line: greater weight does not always require a greater number of attacks.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks become sparse around 1:50–2:15 while relative level rises, supporting the contrast in activity.

cues.title: A lower starting point
cues.text: Across this transition, a quieter, darker stretch becomes the starting point for renewed repeated activity. Compare the reduced sound with the later build-up rather than expecting a named instrument to enter at this note.
cues.evidence: A strong change near 2:24 precedes low relative level and reduced upper-frequency energy, followed by more attacks around 2:30–2:35.

cues.title: Two more ballets
cues.text: Diaghilev’s company followed The Firebird with Petrushka in 1911 and The Rite of Spring in 1913. Their subjects moved from a Russian fairy tale to the life of a puppet and an imagined pagan ritual.
cues.evidence: The Stravinsky Foundation biography dates the three ballets and describes their scenarios.

cues.title: More than one closing surge
cues.text: The later passage rises strongly, retreats and then builds again. Keep following after the first crest: the closing stretch contains more than one change of scale.
cues.evidence: Relative level peaks around 3:35, recedes towards 3:50 and rises again towards 4:00.

cues.title: From attacks to sustained weight
cues.text: Across the closing passage, compare the repeated attacks with the longer final sound. The ending’s sustained weight differs from the clipped gestures of the opening, before the remaining resonance diminishes.
cues.evidence: The highest relative-level window is near 4:00 with little new attack activity, followed by a steep decline after 4:05.

transitions.title: The dance exchanges blows for a line
transitions.how: The clipped figures give way to a longer melodic paragraph, but the dance’s chromatic vocabulary remains: semitone motion and tritone spans still prevent the line from sounding like a new diatonic song. In Knox’s band version, wind and brass sustain the weight that orchestral strings would otherwise help carry. Fewer fresh attacks let the changing harmony beneath the line become more noticeable. The contrast comes from holding sounds across the pulse, not from abandoning the dance for a slow movement.
transitions.evidence: The 1:48 section boundary precedes a fall in detected attack density and brightness around 1:50, while the following sustained span gains level. Marcel Bowman’s dissertation, The Human Versus the Supernatural, pp. 98–99 and 103–05, documents the dance’s semitone and tritone-based motifs: https://collections.lib.utah.edu/dl_files/6e/34/6e3433faa6efb79c80229fe8373f0a7d3aaeab9c.pdf. Commons establishes Knox’s concert-band scoring; the account does not transfer individual string parts to unverified band instruments or assign a new key from the analysis.

transitions.title: The heavy paragraph contracts to low activity
transitions.how: The sustained paragraph is cut back to a quieter, darker layer before short repeated figures begin accumulating again. With less upper-register weight, the lower line becomes more exposed; the rhythm is rebuilt through separate attacks instead of another broad phrase. The familiar chromatic cells connect the new activity to the earlier dance even though its scale has changed. In this band performance the contrast is between differently weighted wind, brass and percussion textures, not between bowed and plucked strings.
transitions.evidence: The 2:24 section boundary is a strong change: relative level drops from about −12.8 dB at 2:20 to −27.5 dB at 2:25, with reduced upper-frequency energy; attacks increase around 2:30–2:35. The repeated chromatic cells are features of Stravinsky’s dance discussed by Bowman. The report cannot establish an exact chord, bass instrument or instrumental entrance at this boundary.

transitions.title: Repeated attacks become sustained weight
transitions.how: The closing build is not one uninterrupted crescendo: a retreat separates its earlier crest from the final expansion. Stravinsky’s repeated gestures then give way to a sound held across the pulse. The bass and upper layers cease their successive attacks, so the band’s sustained weight replaces the dance’s restless articulation. Listen beyond the strongest moment to the dying resonance: the decisive change is the end of renewed rhythmic impulses, not the introduction of a fresh theme.
transitions.evidence: The 4:00 section boundary lies at the highest relative-level window, about −5.9 dB, after the retreat near 3:50. Detected attacks are sparse at 4:00 and absent at 4:05, followed by a steep level decline. The written contrast between active dance figures and the sustained ending supplies the formal reading; no tonic label or transition into the unrecorded Berceuse is asserted.

facts: Russia · Switzerland 1914–20 · France 1920–39 · United States from 1939
Sergei Diaghilev · Vaslav Nijinsky · C. F. Ramuz · George Balanchine · W. H. Auden
Ballets, operas, symphonies, sacred choral music and chamber works; three successive approaches to tonality
composer.background:
Igor Stravinsky grew up in a St Petersburg household in which opera was a profession: his father, Fyodor, was a bass at the Mariinsky Theatre. Born at the family’s summer residence in Oranienbaum in 1882, Igor began piano lessons at ten but entered St Petersburg University to study law. Through a fellow student, Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, he met Vladimir’s father, whose private teaching became more important than a conservatory course. Regular lessons between 1905 and 1908 covered orchestration as practical work: distributing a passage among instruments, then comparing the result with the teacher’s solution. The Symphony in E♭, Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks belong to this apprenticeship, with traces of Tchaikovsky, Alexander Glazunov and the Russian fairy-tale orchestra.

In 1906 he married his cousin Catherine Nossenko; their four children were born between 1907 and 1914. Sergei Diaghilev heard the young composer’s orchestral music in 1909 and first employed him to orchestrate Chopin for Les Sylphides. A larger commission followed: The Firebird, with choreography by Michel Fokine. Its premiere at the Paris Opéra on 25 June 1910, with Tamara Karsavina in the title role, made Stravinsky’s reputation outside Russia. The distinction between human and supernatural characters is audible in the harmony: folk-like diatonic tunes for Ivan and the princesses, chromatic and symmetrical scales for the Firebird and Kashchei. The closing horn melody expands into an orchestral procession without abandoning its short repeating phrases.
composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: A composer of ballets who made the placement of an accent as consequential as a change of harmony.
